ouro.title: Ouro Room
ouro.tagline: A room for music, people, and the moment.
ouro.tldr: I designed and built the Ouro Room website from scratch in React and TypeScript, and I handle the collective’s graphic design and social media. The October 2026 redesign gives each kind of content its own color, swaps placeholder records for real posters and photos, and lets the team add and publish content in a few clicks.
meta: Web developer, graphic designer, social media manager

image.alt: The Ouro Room homepage: upcoming events as poster cards on a starry black background

embed.title: The live Ouro Room website
embed.caption: The live site. Click anywhere to enter, then browse events, artists, mixes, and the gallery.

sections.heading: The collective
sections.body: Ouro Room is a collective I helped found in 2024 after a Boiler Room show. It brings local artists of all kinds together, connecting them with each other and giving them a platform: we book DJs and bands, find venues for them to play, and help them grow their audiences.

sections.heading: The name
sections.body: Ouro comes from the ouroboros, the snake eating its own tail. Music is always changing, and we believe every ending is a new beginning.

sections.heading: What I do
list: Web development: I designed and built the site from scratch in React and TypeScript, with a Django REST API behind it.
Graphic design: I made the logo and visual identity.
Social media: I manage the collective’s social media.

sections.heading: Process
sections.body: The first version launched in June 2025. It worked, but every page looked alike: dark slate panels, one sky-blue accent, and the same vinyl record standing in for artists, mixes, and photos. This recording shows that original site.

video.caption: The original site, before the October 2026 redesign
video.label: Screen recording of the original Ouro Room website: events, DJs, mixes, about, gallery, contact, and admin forms

changes.what: Real posters, photos, and cover art instead of placeholder records
changes.why: Artists, mixes, and the gallery all used the same record graphic, so nothing stood out. Event posters, artist photos, and cover art now show the actual people and nights.

changes.what: A color for each kind of content
changes.why: One accent made events, artists, and mixes look alike. Each type now has its own color, so you can tell what you’re looking at before you read a word.

changes.what: Events up front, in a scrolling rail
changes.why: Upcoming shows are why most people visit, but each event used to take up a full-width panel. Poster cards now sit in a rail with a “Next up” tag, and past events have their own page with links to their photos.
The collective is for artists of all kinds, not only DJs, so the menu now matches who we book.

changes.what: Mixes that play in one shared player
changes.why: Mixes stream from SoundCloud or Spotify, where artists already publish, in a docked player that plays one mix at a time so sound never overlaps.
People come looking for photos from the night they were there, so photos are grouped into an album per event, with a viewer to enlarge, browse, and download them.

changes.what: Admin out of the public menu
changes.why: The original menu showed “Admin” to every visitor. It now sits behind its own sign-in, and the admin itself was redesigned (more below).

sections.heading: Color, before and after
sections.body: Colors pulled from each version’s stylesheet. The original used one sky blue on dark slate panels, and its other colors were tied to button types: teal for back, plum for delete. The redesign keeps the black starfield and white type, and gives each kind of content its own neon accent.
list: Color now tells you what something is (an event, an artist, a mix, an album) instead of what a button does
Near-black cards let the posters and photos carry the color instead of the panels
Louder neon on the same minimal space look matches the sci-fi magazine style of the new event posters

sections.heading: UX principles
sections.body: The redesign is built around helping people find what they came for quickly: the next show, an artist, a mix, or photos from a night.

items.title: Recognition over recall
items.body: Each content type keeps the same color, label, and card layout everywhere, from the home page to the admin.

items.title: Consistency
items.body: Every public card and panel shares one tile style, so once you learn one page you know them all.

items.title: Visibility of status
items.body: A “Next up” tag marks the next event, past events show how many photos they have, and the docked player shows what’s playing.

items.title: Match the real world
items.body: “DJs” became “Artists,” and events link straight to the photos from that night.

items.title: Fewer dead ends
items.body: Artist profiles list their mixes, mix cards link back to the artist, and the photo viewer lets you enlarge, browse, and download without leaving the gallery.

sections.heading: The admin: adding and choosing content
sections.body: The collective adds and updates everything themselves, so the admin had to be quick to learn. It opens on just two choices: Add content and Review & publish.

items.title: Adding
items.body: One form per content type (event, artist, mix, or gallery photos), with dropdowns instead of free typing: a genre list with an Other option, an artist picker for mixes, and an event picker for photos.

items.title: Drafts first
items.body: New uploads stay drafts until someone publishes them, so nothing half-finished goes live by accident.

items.title: Choosing
items.body: Each review page shows how many items are published, and the team picks what’s featured on the home page from there.

items.title: Editing in place
items.body: Change a mix’s artist or genre, move photos between events, or filter the gallery by event right on the review cards, which save as you go.

items.title: Less noise
items.body: Cover art on review cards, no internal ID numbers in labels, and a centered sign-in that’s no longer linked from the public menu.

sections.heading: The identity
sections.body: I designed the logo and visual identity. The Illustrator board below is the messy middle: mood-board references, color swatches, and wordmark tests side by side. From there I narrowed down to the record logo and the motion wordmark, then revised with the team’s feedback.

logos.caption: Motion wordmark

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: How to build a brand around an idea the team cares about, how to take feedback without losing the core concept, and what it takes to start something from nothing.

hyperdrive.title: Hyperdrive
hyperdrive.tagline: Making a club’s finances and equipment easier to navigate.
hyperdrive.tldr: Hyperdrive is the internal tool CU Boulder’s Hyperloop team uses to track equipment, inventory, contacts, expenses, and budgets. It was built for function first. I brought a design eye to it: tables that line up, spending you can see at a glance, and a look that matches the Hyperloop brand.

image.alt: Hyperdrive home screen: Welcome to Hyperdrive over a photo of the tunnel boring machine, with buttons for each part of the tool

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: The team’s spreadsheets moved into Hyperdrive, but the tables were hard to read. Columns drifted out of line across the full width, so a part’s cost could sit under the wrong header, and expanding a row broke the layout. Spending only existed as rows of numbers.

pairs.title: Master Equipment List

before.caption: Columns drift out of line

after.alt: After: the equipment table with every column aligned under its header and a filter panel on top
after.caption: Every column lines up

pairs.note: I gave each column a fixed width so headers and values line up across the whole table. The list also gained a filter panel to search and narrow parts by school year.

pairs.title: Opening a part

before.alt: Before: expanding a row pushes a blank gray bar through the table
before.caption: Expanding a row breaks the table

after.alt: After: expanding a row shows its purchases nested underneath, still aligned
after.caption: Purchases nest underneath

pairs.note: Opening a part now shows its purchases nested right under it, without breaking the rows around it.

sections.heading: From rows to a picture: the data visualization
sections.body: Expenses are logged one purchase at a time. The budget view turns that same money into a summary anyone on the team can read in seconds: what came in, what went out, and the balance over time.

figures.caption: Expenses: every purchase as a row

sections.heading: What I did
list: Built visualizations of the club’s spending: summary totals and a chart of inflow, outflow, and balance
Redesigned the interface for accessibility and readability, using Mantine components
Fixed the Master Equipment List so its columns line up
Brought the tool in line with the Hyperloop brand I designed for the club’s marketing
Wrote documentation on what the tool is for, its features, and how it works

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: How much small layout fixes, like column widths, change whether people trust a tool, and how to carry one brand from print into software.

ux-audit.title: DonorsChoose UX Audit
ux-audit.tagline: Finding ways to make classroom giving easier to navigate.
ux-audit.tldr: For UX Design 2, a course in my UX certificate, I audited DonorsChoose against Nielsen’s heuristics and WCAG. The site has strong foundations; the biggest opportunities are clearer wayfinding, consistent calls to action, and a handful of accessibility fixes.

image.alt: Title slide for the DonorsChoose UX audit presentation

embed.title: The full DonorsChoose UX audit (PDF)
embed.caption: The full audit, 25 pages. Scroll inside the frame to read it.

meta: Heuristics, WCAG review, persona + user flow

sections.heading: The question
sections.body: How might DonorsChoose make it easier for teachers to find support and for donors to confidently fund a classroom? I reviewed key journeys through the public platform, with attention to the homepage, Find a Classroom, About Us, Partner with Us, and Help Center.

sections.heading: How I evaluated it
list: Reviewed the experience against Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics
Evaluated screen-reader order, keyboard navigation, focus visibility, and color contrast
Mapped the information architecture and a donor’s path to supporting a classroom
Created a donor persona and reviewed visual design, content, and navigation

sections.heading: What I found
list: Strong foundations: clear typography, generous whitespace, helpful teacher information, and keyboard-accessible controls with visible focus
Wayfinding gaps: internal pages often lacked back navigation or clear location cues, making it hard to retrace a path
Unclear calls to action: similar actions used inconsistent labels, and some links led to overlapping information
Accessibility refinements: improve CTA hover contrast, remove redundant nested links and unhelpful status markers, and clarify filter behavior
Mobile opportunity: shorten long pages and address the map layering issue identified in the audit

sections.heading: Priorities
sections.body: I prioritized navigation dropdowns and page context, simpler and less repetitive content paths, visible back navigation, and clearer filter rules. Medium-priority improvements included standardizing CTA language, moving teacher stories higher, and increasing hover-state contrast. The audit also calls out strengths to preserve, including keyboard navigation, visible focus, and the platform’s warm visual language.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: How to separate the strengths worth keeping from the problems, and how to turn a long list of findings into a few priorities a team can act on.

outcome.text: for DonorsChoose: navigation and page context, simpler content paths, visible back navigation, and clearer filter rules.

aldente.title: Al Dente
aldente.tagline: A recipe app with an e-ink hardware extension, still cooking.
aldente.tldr: In progress, wrapping up April 2027. My capstone team is building a recipe app for storing recipes, with an e-ink hardware extension. After user testing, we’ll evaluate what the community actually needs.

sections.heading: What we’re building
sections.body: Al Dente is a recipe app for storing your recipes, with an e-ink hardware extension. After user testing, we’ll evaluate what the community needs and shape the app around it.

sections.heading: The goal
sections.body: Have the app fully functioning on modern tech that keeps it efficient, with our focus on the implementation. Alongside it, we’re creating a mock brand through real beta testing, and documenting the iteration process thoroughly.

sections.heading: Early findings
sections.body: From our first interviews with home cooks, and what each finding changed.
rows: Most recipes come from social media, scattered across Instagram saves, Pinterest, bookmarks, and docs, with no single home
Our first challenge: turning a social media post into a complete recipe stored in the app to revisit or reshare
Most people cook from digital recipes, but scrolling between ingredients and steps, ads, and a screen that dims are frustrating
A step-by-step cook mode with ingredients inside each step, plus the e-ink cookbook for a calm, distraction-free page
Family recipes came up in 3 of 4 early interviews and carry emotional weight
A space for family recipes with stories, photos, and loose measurements like “a handful”
People already coordinate in WhatsApp, iMessage, and GroupMe and like them
Dinner invites that drop into existing group chats instead of replacing them
A participant nearly started a fire by forgetting bread in the oven
Timers tied to specific steps and an “oven still on?” reminder at the end

sections.heading: Follow along
sections.body: The capstone team posts progress on Instagram while the app comes together.
sections.label: @aldentecapstone on Instagram

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: How to ask questions without steering people, how a surprise finding can become a team’s first design problem, and how to recruit real participants beyond my own friends.

outcome.text: beta with real community members, after App Store submission, to measure whether the app meets what people need.
